opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's something I think about a lot. With the original Genie, we had three main pieces: the video tokenizer, the latent action model, and the dynamics model that predicts the next frame autoregressively given the past frames and an action. A lot of the cost comes from operating over many tokens per frame and running several sampling steps for each new frame. So I see a few natural directions.

The first is the tokenizer. If you can compress video into a more compact, semantically meaningful latent space, everything downstream gets cheaper. Right now much of the representation goes toward reconstructing pixel detail that may not matter for the dynamics. If the model could spend its capacity on what actually changes, like the character moving or the platform shifting, and represent static background more cheaply, you'd save a lot of compute.

The second is the sampling process. We used a MaskGIT-style approach, which is already more parallel than pure token-by-token generation, but you still iterate. People have had a lot of success distilling diffusion and masked models down to very few steps, and I think something similar could work for world models. That matters especially for interactivity, because if you want someone to actually play in one of these generated worlds, you need something close to real time.

Third is memory and context. As you generate longer sequences, attending over the full history gets expensive, and you also start to see consistency issues. Smarter memory mechanisms, whether that's some form of compressed state, caching, or recurrent-style components, could help with both efficiency and long-horizon coherence.

Finally, I'm interested in exploiting structure in the action space. The latent action model learns a small, discrete set of actions without any labels, and that's a strong signal about what's controllable in a scene. You could imagine using it to focus computation on the parts of the frame the action actually affects, rather than regenerating everything uniformly.

None of these is a single silver bullet, but together I think they could take these models from impressive research demos to something people can interact with fluidly. That's the exciting part for me: once generation is cheap and fast enough, these become environments you can train agents in at scale, not just videos you watch.

r001.rationale: The response proposes compressed state, caching, and recurrent-style memory, but does not identify state space models as an approach.

r002.rationale: It mentions many tokens per frame, but does not explain that image patches serve the Transformer's need for tokens to predict.

r003.rationale: It discusses distilling diffusion and masked models to fewer steps and separately proposes compact latents, but does not propose diffusion over latent representations as an alternative to predicting image patches.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a great question, and it's something we think about a lot. So just to set the stage a bit, Genie is this generative interactive environment model, and the way it works right now is we have basically three components. There's a video tokenizer that compresses the frames into discrete tokens, there's a latent action model that learns actions in an unsupervised way just from watching video, and then there's the dynamics model, which is the thing that actually predicts the next frame given the past frames and the latent action.

And the dynamics model right now is a spatiotemporal transformer, which, you know, it's great because it's really flexible and it scales well, but it's also expensive. Every time you generate a frame you're attending over all the previous frames and all the spatial tokens, and that cost grows as the context grows. So if you want long rollouts, or you want it to run in real time so someone can actually play in it, that's where the efficiency question really bites.

So I think there are a few directions. One is just on the tokenizer side. Right now we're using a pretty standard VQ-VAE setup, and if you can get a more compressed representation, fewer tokens per frame while still keeping the information you need for the dynamics, that helps everything downstream almost for free. There's a lot of work on better temporal compression, where you're not re-encoding things that haven't changed much between frames, and I think that's really promising.

The second is on the dynamics model itself. You could imagine moving away from full attention over the whole history toward something more like a recurrent state, or at least a bounded memory, so the cost per step is roughly constant. There's been a lot of interesting work on state space models and hybrid architectures, and for an interactive setting that's kind of the natural fit, because you really do want this notion of "here's my current world state, here's an action, give me the next state."

And then the third thing, which I think is maybe the most exciting, is thinking about the latent action model more carefully. Right now the actions are learned to be discrete and fairly small in number, which is nice because it makes the controllability very clean. But if the actions capture more of the structure of what changes between frames, then the dynamics model has less work to do. You're sort of factorizing the problem so that the hard part, the "what's going to happen," is more cleanly separated from the "render it."

So I'd say the overall direction is to push more of the work into learning good, compact representations, both of the frames and of the actions, so that the generation step itself can be lighter. And honestly the thing that made Genie work in the first place was being able to train on a huge amount of unlabeled internet video, so any efficiency gain also means we can scale that data and the model size further, which tends to be where the biggest improvements come from.

r001.rationale: It proposes state space models or bounded memory to make per-step generation cheaper for long rollouts.

r002.rationale: It mentions discrete tokens and spatial tokens, but does not clearly identify an image-patch representation as tokens the Transformer predicts.

r003.rationale: It does not mention diffusion over latent representations as an alternative.

astra-6.text:
I think one promising direction is to do more of the modeling in a compressed latent space, rather than predicting every pixel. Video has a lot of redundancy across frames, so ideally the model would represent what’s changing without having to regenerate all of the information about the scene at every step.

For something like Genie, you also want to preserve the connection between actions and what happens next. So the question is: how compact can you make that representation while still capturing the details that matter for interaction? You could imagine a model that predicts the broader dynamics at a lower temporal resolution, with another component filling in the visual details. That could reduce computation, but you’d have to check that it still responds accurately to actions and stays consistent over time.

r001.rationale: The response suggests compressed latent representations and lower temporal resolution, but it does not mention state space models or clearly connect that approach to longer generations.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss Genie’s image patch representation or explain that it provides tokens for the Transformer to predict.

r003.rationale: It proposes modeling in a compressed latent space, but does not identify diffusion over latent representations as an alternative to predicting image patches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one promising direction is to separate what you need to model about the world from what you need to render. If you’re predicting every visual detail at every time step, that’s expensive. But a lot of what’s in a scene persists, so you could imagine learning a compact representation of the state, predicting how that changes with an action, and then decoding it into video.

You could also make that representation hierarchical, with slower updates for the overall scene and faster updates for things that are moving. The question is how much you can compress while preserving the details that matter for interaction. For something like Genie, efficiency isn’t just about producing frames faster; it’s about keeping the world coherent and responsive to what the user does.

r001.rationale: It proposes a compact state representation and hierarchical updates, but does not mention state space models or longer video generations.

r002.rationale: It discusses representing scene state compactly, but does not mention image patches or the Transformer's need for prediction tokens.

r003.rationale: It suggests decoding a state representation into video, but does not identify diffusion over latent representations as an alternative to predicting image patches.
